BFF
BEE-ef-EF
noun (Millennial slang)
Initialism for best friends forever, written in yearbooks and on notes passed in class since at least the 1980s, then universal in 2000s texting, MySpace "Top 8" friend rankings, and girls’ jewellery (the split-heart "BE FRI / ST ENDS" necklace). Paris Hilton’s reality show My New BFF (2008) marked the peak, and the major dictionaries admitted BFF in the early 2010s. Variants: bestie, BFFL (best friends for life).

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

A BFF is one’s best friend, sealed with the word forever. The initialism belongs to adolescence, especially to girls, and to the age of the ranked friend list, when a MySpace Top 8 could make or break a week. The Christian observation: the longing in the word is good and old. Scripture prizes deep friendship and gives us its great portrait. "The soul of Jonathan was knit with the soul of David, and Jonathan loved him as his own soul" (1Sa 18:1). "A friend loveth at all times, and a brother is born for adversity" (Pro 17:17). "There is a friend that sticketh closer than a brother" (Pro 18:24). The word’s weakness is the forever. Adolescent BFFs change with the school year, and the ranked list taught a generation that friendship is a status to be displayed and revised. Real friendship is proved over years and through trouble: "Faithful are the wounds of a friend" (Pro 27:6). And the only forever friendship on offer belongs to Christ: "Henceforth I call you not servants … but I have called you friends" (Joh 15:15). A father tells his daughter: a true friend is one who will tell you the truth and stay; pray for one, and be one. He tells his son: men need friends too, and the friend worth having will sharpen you, as iron sharpeneth iron.

Webster 1828 Definition

Millennial initialism (1980s notes → 2000s texting) for best friends forever; redeemable as a longing for covenant friendship like David and Jonathan’s, whose only true forever is Christ’s friendship (Joh 15:15).

BFF, n. (Millennial slang, 1980s–2010s; initialism of best friends forever) One’s closest friend. "She’s my BFF." Also bestie, BFFL; the split-heart BFF necklace.

Culture: MySpace "Top 8," My New BFF (2008); in the major dictionaries by the early 2010s.

Webster (1828), root friend: FRIEND, noun frend. 1. One who is attached to another by affection; one who entertains for another sentiments of esteem, respect and affection, which lead him to desire his company, and to seek to promote his happiness and prosperity; opposed to foe or enemy. A friend loveth at all times. Proverbs 17:17 . 2. One not hostile; opposed to an enemy in war. 3. One reconciled after enmity. Let us be friends again. 4. An attendant; a companion. 5. A favorer; one who is propitious; as a friend to commerce; a friend to poetry; […]

Decode for parents: teach your children to choose friends who sharpen them and to be the friend who stays.

Key Scripture

1Sa 18:1 — "And it came to pass, when he had made an end of speaking unto Saul, that the soul of Jonathan was knit with the soul of David, and Jonathan loved him as his own soul."

Pro 17:17 — "A friend loveth at all times, and a brother is born for adversity."

Pro 18:24 — "A man that hath friends must shew himself friendly: and there is a friend that sticketh closer than a brother."

Pro 27:6 — "Faithful are the wounds of a friend; but the kisses of an enemy are deceitful."

Joh 15:15 — "Henceforth I call you not servants; for the servant knoweth not what his lord doeth: but I have called you friends; for all things that I have heard of my Father I have made known unto you."

Modern Corruption

BFF turns friendship into a ranked, revisable status; Scripture’s friendship is a covenant proved in adversity, and its only true forever is the friendship of Christ.

expand to see more

The corruption came with the ranking. When friendship became a public list, it became a status game: who is in, who has been demoted, who is everyone’s BFF this month. Girls especially learned that friendship is a performance and that "forever" lasts until the next falling-out. The word promises a covenant and delivers a popularity chart, and the wound of being dropped from it is real.

The recovery is covenant friendship. Jonathan made a covenant with David and kept it at the cost of a throne; Ruth said to Naomi, "whither thou goest, I will go" (Rut 1:16) and meant it. Teach the young that friends are made by faithfulness, not by declaration; that a friend who wounds you with the truth loves you more than one who flatters; and that the Friend who laid down His life for His friends is the one whose forever is real.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Old English freond (one who loves) → best friends forever → 1980s notes and yearbooks → 2000s texting, MySpace Top 8 → dictionaries, early 2010s.

Old English freond, from freogan — to love, to favour

1980s: yearbook and note-passing initialism BFF

2000s: texting, MySpace Top 8, split-heart necklaces; My New BFF (2008)

Early 2010s: entered the major dictionaries; bestie as the spoken form

Biblical anchor: the soul of Jonathan was knit with the soul of David (1Sa 18:1); I have called you friends (Joh 15:15)
